Brief impact on oyster suitability: Controls feeding, growth, reproduction, recruitment, disease, predation, and survival; suitability declines under prolonged very low or very high salinity.
Regulates metabolism, filtration, growth, spawning, and larval development; thermal extremes increase physiological stress and can intensify low-oxygen effects.
Stable hard substrate supports larval attachment and reef persistence, whereas soft or rapidly accumulating sediments can bury or destabilize oysters.
Adequate oxygen supports respiration, feeding, and growth, while persistent hypoxia or anoxia suppresses performance and can cause mortality.
Water movement regulates salinity and transports larvae, oxygen, and food, but excessive currents or altered freshwater inflow can reduce settlement or create unsuitable conditions.
Depth influences exposure, temperature, oxygen conditions, and restoration feasibility; overly shallow or deep settings can limit reef persistence or access.
High suspended-sediment loads can interfere with filtration and settlement, while deposition can smother oysters or cover suitable substrate.
Phytoplankton availability supports filtration and growth, whereas insufficient food constrains production and excessive enrichment may contribute to oxygen stress.
